title: Japan Arrival Checklist for Digital Nomads (2026)

phases.title: Before You Fly
phases.description: Most of this you can't fix once you land. Do it before you fly.

items.label: Confirm your visa type
items.description: ~73 countries get visa-free tourist entry (mofa.go.jp). 90 days for most Western countries, 30 days for Brunei, 15 days for Indonesia and Thailand (ePassport required). UAE upgraded to 90 days as of July 2025. DN visa (up to 6 months) requires ¥10M+ annual income and a non-Japanese employer. Work/resident visas require a Certificate of Eligibility (COE).
tips: Certificate of Eligibility (COE) is optional but speeds up DN visa processing — takes 1-3 months to obtain, start early
Most visitors enter visa-free; DN visa is for those wanting full 6-month compliance
Work visa holders: COE must be issued before you apply at a Japanese consulate
items.linkLabel: Japan DN Visa vs Tourist Visa (2026)

items.label: Get an eSIM before boarding
items.description: Ubigi, Airalo, or Mobal all work. Activate after landing. Skips the physical SIM kiosk queue at Narita.
tips: Physical SIM kiosks exist at Narita and Haneda but lines can be long on busy arrival evenings
Activate on airport WiFi first, then switch to eSIM

items.label: Download LINE, PayPay, Navitime, Tabelog
items.description: Four essential apps before you land:
tips: LINE: messaging — Japan's WhatsApp, except everyone actually uses it
PayPay: QR payments at restaurants, konbini, vending machines
Navitime: train navigation — handles transfers better than Google Maps
Tabelog: restaurant reviews — the real ones, not tourist traps

items.label: Get a medication letter for prescription drugs
items.description: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing each medication, dosage, and generic name. Some common drugs (pseudoephedrine, certain ADHD meds) are controlled in Japan.
warnings: Some common medications including pseudoephedrine and certain ADHD drugs are controlled substances in Japan — check Ministry of Health import rules before packing

items.label: Pack your document folder
items.description: Passport (6+ months validity), visa approval if applicable, accommodation confirmation with address in Japanese, travel insurance proof, 2 passport photos.
tips: Print accommodation address in Japanese characters — taxi drivers and station staff may not read romaji

items.label: Book accommodation for 1-2 weeks only
items.description: Neighborhoods feel different in person. Don't lock into a 3-month lease sight unseen.
tips: Shinjuku is loud; Shimokitazawa is walkable; Koenji is cheap and eclectic
Explore neighborhoods before committing to a longer-term rental
items.linkLabel: Japan Digital Nomad Housing: The Catch-22

items.label: Notify your home bank of Japan travel
items.description: Prevents card freezes at convenience store ATMs on arrival day.
warnings: A frozen card at a 7-Eleven ATM on day one can stall your entire arrival sequence

phases.title: Day 0: Airport
phases.description: Run this sequence in order. Each step sets up the next.

items.label: Clear immigration
items.description: Have passport, return/onward ticket info, and accommodation address ready. Visa-free entry gets a 90-day stamp. DN visa holders show visa and COE if applicable.

items.label: Receive Residence Card (在留カード) at immigration
items.description: At 7 major airports (NRT, HND, KIX, FUK, NGO, CTS, HIJ), residence cards are issued at the immigration counter on Day 0. You will need this for ward office registration.
tips: Issued automatically at NRT/HND/KIX/FUK/NGO/CTS/HIJ — no separate queue
If arriving at a smaller airport, your card will be mailed to your registered address later

items.label: Activate eSIM (or grab physical SIM)
items.description: Connect to free airport WiFi first, then activate eSIM. Send one LINE message to confirm it works before leaving the airport.
tips: Physical SIM kiosks are in the arrivals hall if you didn't get an eSIM pre-flight

items.label: Get a Suica card
items.description: Pick the right option for your situation:
tips: Apple Wallet Suica (iPhone 8+): 10-year validity, load ¥3,000 with Mastercard/Amex — best for most visitors
Welcome Suica (physical card): 28-day validity, no deposit, non-refundable balance at expiry
Welcome Suica Mobile app: 180-day validity, English interface, good for longer tourist stays
Mobile Suica app (residents only): Japanese-only, needed for commuter passes (定期券)
Apple Wallet Suica goes dormant after 6 months of non-use — ask station staff to reactivate

items.label: Withdraw ¥30,000–50,000 cash
items.description: 7-Eleven ATMs accept most international cards and display English. Pull cash before leaving the airport.
tips: Small ramen shops, izakayas, temples, and street vendors are often cash-only
7-Eleven ATMs are everywhere so you won't run out of options, but having cash from the start avoids friction

items.label: Get to your accommodation
items.description: From Narita:
tips: Narita → NEX: ¥3,250, ~60 min to Tokyo/Shinjuku/Shibuya
Narita → Skyliner: ¥2,580, ~41 min to Ueno
Narita → Limousine bus: ¥3,200, direct to major hotels
Haneda → Monorail: ¥500, ~15 min / Keikyu line: ¥330, ~20 min
Arriving after 11pm? Last trains are gone — budget for taxi or airport hotel

phases.title: Days 1–3: Ward Office
phases.description: Resident visa holders must register at the ward office (区役所/市役所). This single step unlocks NHI, ゆうちょ bank, and contract SIM.

items.label: Register at ward office (住民登録)
items.description: Bring your Residence Card and passport to the local ward office (区役所/市役所). Registration is legally required within 14 days of arrival. You will receive a 住民票 (juminhyo) which is required for banking and insurance.
tips: Bring Residence Card + passport — both required
Some ward offices have English-speaking staff; call ahead if unsure
You'll receive a 住民票 (juminhyo) — keep several copies, needed for bank and insurance applications
warnings: DN visa holders do NOT receive a Residence Card and cannot do ward registration — use private health insurance instead
Short-term tourists are also ineligible for ward registration

items.label: Enroll in National Health Insurance (国民健康保険)
items.description: Apply at the ward office — same visit as registration. NHI covers 70% of medical costs; premiums are income-based (first year is typically low).
tips: Premiums are calculated on previous year's income — first year abroad is often the cheapest
Apply on the same day as ward registration — no separate appointment needed
warnings: DN visa holders are not eligible for NHI — maintain private travel or health insurance instead

items.label: Pick up the English garbage guide at the ward office
items.description: Free, practical, and saves you from bin-day confusion for the rest of your stay.

phases.title: Week 1–2: Banking & SIM
phases.description: Get banking and long-term connectivity sorted. Residents open ゆうちょ bank after ward registration; tourists and DN visa holders use international cards and prepaid SIMs.

items.label: Test WiFi speed at your accommodation
items.description: 25+ Mbps minimum for video calls. Verify before unpacking — you need to know if you need a backup plan.

items.label: Open ゆうちょ銀行 (Japan Post Bank) account
items.description: Easiest Japanese bank for new residents — no 6-month wait, foreign-friendly. Bring Residence Card, passport, and your 住民票 to any post office branch.
tips: No minimum balance; free cash withdrawals at 7-Eleven ATMs nationwide
Required for salary transfer if working in Japan
Process takes about 30–60 minutes at a post office branch
US citizens: FATCA disclosure required (US-Japan IGA, 2013). Bring passport + Social Security number. Online application is typically blocked — must visit in person.
warnings: Regular banks (SMBC, MUFG) typically require 6+ months of residence — start with ゆうちょ

items.label: Switch to a contract SIM (Rakuten, IIJmio, or similar)
items.description: Contract SIMs require resident registration. Rakuten Mobile is cheapest (¥3,168/mo unlimited). IIJmio for lower data needs.
tips: Rakuten: ¥3,168/mo unlimited, requires Residence Card + bank account
IIJmio: from ¥858/mo for 2GB — good for WiFi-primary users
Tourists and DN visa holders: stick with prepaid SIM or eSIM

items.label: Set up PayPay
items.description: Link your international card and test it at a konbini. Once it works, you'll use it at restaurants, konbini, and vending machines everywhere.
tips: Test with a small konbini purchase first to confirm your card links correctly

items.label: Walk to nearest konbini, supermarket, and train station
items.description: Orient yourself on foot. Knowing these three locations solves most day-to-day logistics.

items.label: Get garbage collection schedule
items.description: Check the building notice board or ask your landlord. Japan takes garbage separation seriously — wrong bag on wrong day causes real friction with neighbors.
tips: Combustible, non-combustible, recyclables, and large items all have separate collection days and bag colors
items.linkLabel: Japan Garbage Rules: A Foreigner's Guide

items.label: Download Safety Tips and Yahoo! Bosai
items.description: Safety Tips is a multilingual government disaster alert app. Yahoo! Bosai adds earthquake early warnings. Both are essential in Japan.
items.linkLabel: Japan Earthquake Guide for Digital Nomads

items.label: Locate your nearest evacuation point (避難場所)
items.description: Your ward office has maps. Identify the hinanbasho nearest to your accommodation before you need it.
tips: Evacuation points are typically parks, schools, or public facilities

items.label: Test a coworking space with a day pass
items.description: WeWork, Regus, or a local spot. Check WiFi speed and outlet availability before committing to a monthly plan.
tips: Monthly coworking runs ¥15,000–30,000 — worth vetting before committing

items.label: Attend a meetup, coworking event, or language exchange
items.description: Tokyo Meetup groups are active. Osaka has a smaller but friendlier scene.
tips: Language exchanges are a good entry point even if your Japanese is zero

phases.title: Month 1+: Long-term Setup
phases.description: For residents settling in long-term. My Number card and regular banking arrive later — neither is a blocker for daily life.

items.label: Apply for My Number card (マイナンバーカード)
items.description: My Number is assigned automatically at ward registration; the physical card takes 6–10 weeks. Used for tax filing, government services, and health insurance verification. Not a gate — get it when convenient.
tips: Apply online at myna.go.jp after receiving your notification letter
Card is useful but not essential in first months — services work with the number alone
Required for e-Tax filing from 2026

items.label: Open a regular bank account (SMBC / MUFG)
items.description: Regular banks require 6+ months of documented residence. Optional — ゆうちょ handles most everyday needs.
tips: SMBC and MUFG have English online banking interfaces
Required for some employer salary transfers that don't accept ゆうちょ

items.label: Run your commute route during rush hour
items.description: Test the route once at peak time so you know what you're in for before a real deadline.
